To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the HSV TK gene can be transferred into cells by two methods: by the introduction of virus DNA and by the use of cell DNA.
the thymidine kinase enzyme of HSV 1 is present in mouse cells transformed with HSV 1 DNA, and the HSV 1 gene responsible for this enzyme is capable of being transmitted from cell to cell in culture.

the thymidine kinase of herpes simplex virus 1 can be introduced into mouse cells by using either the virus DNA or DNA from virus-transformed cells, and that this introduction results in the production of a functional enzyme.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a method of introducing a gene from one species of organism into a cell of another species.
the development of a new system for the study of herpes simplex virus DNA in cells and the introduction of a new gene into cells by using virus DNA or virus-transformed cell DNA.
the development of methods to study the structure of the HSV genome and to investigate the mechanisms of viral gene expression in eukaryotic cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HSV thymidine-kinase gene is introduced into mouse cells using viral DNA or DNA extracted from HSV-transformed cells.
the thymidine kinase activity of the cells is due to the HSV gene and that the cells are transformed by the HSV DNA.
the HSV thymidine gene has been introduced into mouse cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a system for transferring the HSV thymidine gene to mammalian cells, and we have shown that the HSV thymine kinase gene is expressed and is functional in these cells.
the thymidine kinase of the herpes simplex viruses is a useful marker for the introduction of viral genes into cells, and that this enzyme is not present in the normal mouse cell genome.   1
the HSV DNA in transformed cells has a structure which is more similar to the structure of the HSV DNA in the cell nucleus than it is to the structure of HSV DNA in virus particles.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the thymidine kinase-positive phenotype can be introduced into mouse cells using either virus DNA or transformed-cell DNA and that the HSV thymidine enzyme is functional when introduced into cells by either procedure.
the thymidine kinase of HSV can be introduced into mouse cells and expressed in a stable manner, and that the gene is not lost when the cells are propagated for long periods of time.

HSV thymidine-kinase-positive cells are not necessarily transformed cells, and that the thymidine kinase activity found in HSV-transformed cells is HSV-specific, and not the host cell thymidine kinase.
